output.brief: The stops are not caused by the agency temps. They come from a combination of two changes. The 6.4 firmware now keeps weak short-range sensor returns, and the new glossy stretch film produces those returns at oblique angles. Together they make the robots see obstacles that aren't there. Evidence: in the bench test with no people present, 6.4 with gloss film stopped 17 of 20 passes. 6.3 with gloss film stopped 1 of 20, and 6.4 with the old matte film stopped 0 of 20. In the fleet data, only the 6.4 pallet robots in the wrapped-pallet zones rose (3.2 to 15.6 stops per 100 hours). The 6.3 robots working the same zones and shifts stayed flat. The tote robots on 6.4, where no wrapped pallets are staged, also stayed flat. The temps were present for all of these robots, so they do not explain the difference. Confidence is high. What to do: switch back to the previous matte film now, keep the firmware as is, and track stops weekly by zone and firmware group. If the film can't be changed quickly, rolling the pallet robots back to 6.3 is a fallback, but only under the time-limited waiver, because 6.3 security support ends 31 October. Don't shorten the protective fields, and don't adopt the strike policy. Don't count on the December release until it has been tested against this film. The link between stops and missed cut-offs is unproven, since volume rose 18% and cut-off misses also rose last year.
